p.s: Values to pass to the OnServerInvoke callback.

r.s: Values returned from the OnServerInvoke callback.

kid.simple: A LocalScript asks the server a question and waits for the answer. Returns whatever the server's `OnServerInvoke` returns.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local canEnter = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("CanEnterVIP")

if canEnter:InvokeServer() then
	print("Welcome to the VIP room!")
else
	print("Sorry, VIP only.")
end

m.d:
This callback is called when the RemoteFunction is invoked with InvokeClient(). When the bound function returns, the returned values are sent back to the calling server.

See Remote Events and Callbacks for code samples and further details on OnClientInvoke.
m.s: Callback for when the `Class.RemoteFunction` is invoked with `Class.RemoteFunction:InvokeClient()|InvokeClient()`.

p.s: The parameters sent through InvokeClient().

r.s: Values returned by the callback function.

kid.simple: The function a LocalScript sets to answer when the server calls `InvokeClient`. Whatever it returns goes back to the server.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local askSetting = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("AskSetting")

askSetting.OnClientInvoke = function()
	return "dark mode"
end
kid.gotcha: The server should not believe this answer for anything important; the client can lie.

m.d:
This callback is called when the RemoteFunction is invoked with InvokeServer(). When the bound function returns, the returned values are sent back to the calling client.

See Remote Events and Callbacks for code samples and further details on OnServerInvoke.
m.s: Callback for when the `Class.RemoteFunction` is invoked with `Class.RemoteFunction:InvokeServer()|InvokeServer()`.

p.s: The Player associated with the client that the InvokeServer() call originates from.
The parameters sent through InvokeServer().

r.s: Values returned by the callback function.

kid.simple: The function the server sets to answer when a client calls `InvokeServer`. Roblox gives you the player first, then the client's values. Whatever you return goes back to the client.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local getPrice = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("GetPrice")

local PRICES = { Sword = 50, Shield = 30 }

getPrice.OnServerInvoke = function(player, itemName)
	if typeof(itemName) ~= "string" then
		return nil -- bad request, answer nothing
	end
	return PRICES[itemName]
end
kid.gotcha: Only one function can be set. Setting it again replaces the old one.

kid.simple: A RemoteFunction lets a player's device ask the server a question and wait for the answer. Unlike a RemoteEvent, the script that asks stops and waits until the other side replies.
kid.analogy: A RemoteFunction is like calling the shop on the phone and asking 'how much is the sword?'. You stay on the line until they answer. A RemoteEvent is more like sending a text and moving on.
whenToUse: The client needs information only the server knows, like 'what is in my inventory?' or 'did my purchase work?'.
You want a yes/no reply from the server before updating the screen.
Avoid using it to ask a client for something (server asking client). It is risky; see the gotchas.
kid.where: Create it in Studio and put it in ReplicatedStorage. The server sets `OnServerInvoke`; LocalScripts call `InvokeServer`.

terms.server: The one computer, run by Roblox in a data center, that is in charge of a game. Every player in the same game is connected to it. It keeps the official copy of the game, like who has how many coins.
terms.client: Your own device (phone, PC, Xbox) running the game. Every player has their own client. The client draws the screen and reads your keyboard, mouse or touch.
terms.client-server boundary: The invisible wall between the server and each client. They are different computers, so a script on one side cannot just reach over and change a variable on the other side. Messages have to be sent across.
terms.Script: A script that runs on the server. Put it in ServerScriptService.
terms.LocalScript: A script that runs on one player's client. Put it in StarterPlayerScripts, StarterGui or StarterCharacterScripts.
terms.ReplicatedStorage: A storage folder that both the server and every client can see. The usual home for RemoteEvents and RemoteFunctions.
terms.exploiter: A cheater who uses hacking tools to change their own client. They can run any code they want on their own device, including firing your RemoteEvents with fake values.
terms.validate: To double-check something before trusting it. The server validates a request by asking: is this a real item? Can this player afford it? Are they close enough?
terms.invoke: To call a function and wait for its answer.
terms.callback: A function you hand to Roblox so Roblox can run it later. For a RemoteFunction you set the callback with `=`, not with `:Connect`.
terms.yield: To pause a script and wait. `InvokeServer` yields until the server sends back an answer.
terms.return: Handing a value back from a function. Whatever your callback returns is the answer the other side receives.

examples.title: Ask the server how many coins I have
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService + LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts, RemoteFunction named GetCoins in ReplicatedStorage
examples.code:
-- SERVER
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local getCoins = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("GetCoins")

local coinsByUserId = {} -- the server's true record

-- Set the callback with = (only one callback can exist)
getCoins.OnServerInvoke = function(player)
	return coinsByUserId[player.UserId] or 0
end

-- CLIENT
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local getCoins = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("GetCoins")

local coins = getCoins:InvokeServer() -- waits for the answer
print("I have " .. coins .. " coins")
explain: The server sets `OnServerInvoke` to a function. Roblox passes the asking player first.
The LocalScript calls `InvokeServer()` and pauses until the server's function returns.
The returned number arrives on the client and gets printed.

gotchas: Set `OnServerInvoke` with `=`, not `:Connect`. Only the last one you set is used.
Avoid `InvokeClient`. If the player leaves, the server gets an error; if a cheater never answers, the server script waits forever.
Never trust the values the client sends to `InvokeServer`. Check them on the server.
Because the caller waits, a slow server callback freezes the calling LocalScript until it finishes.

class/RenderSettings.d: RenderSettings is a singleton class which lets developers debug components of Roblox's graphics engine. It can be found in Roblox Studio's settings under the Rendering tab.
class/RenderSettings.s: A singleton settings class that exposes rendering configuration for graphics quality, framerate management, and debug visualization in Roblox Studio.

m.d: Sets the starting quality level of the framerate manager when EnableFRM is set to true.
m.s: Sets the starting quality level of the framerate manager.

m.d: When set to true, all scene updates will be given an unlimited budget, regardless of how computationally expensive it may be. This ensures each frame will look as it should, at the cost of a more unstable frame rate.
m.s: Whether all scene updates will be given an unlimited budget, regardless of how computationally expensive it may be.

m.d: Sets the graphics quality level in Roblox Studio when EnableFRM is set to false.
m.s: Sets the graphics quality level in Roblox Studio.

m.d: When set to true, virtual reality (VR) mode is enabled. This property reflects the same underlying setting as UserGameSettings.VREnabled, so reading or writing it reads or writes that shared value. Defaults to false.
m.s: Toggles whether virtual reality (VR) mode is enabled.

m.d:
When set to true, the framerate manager (FRM) dynamically adjusts the rendering quality level during gameplay to maintain a stable framerate. When set to false, the quality level is fixed at RenderSettings.EditQualityLevel and no automatic adjustment occurs. Defaults to true.

The AutoFRMLevel property reports the current quality level that the FRM has assigned when this property is enabled.
m.s: Toggles the enabled state of the framerate manager.

m.d: Controls how materials are written during .obj export from Studio. When set to true, parts that share the same material appearance are merged into shared material definitions in the exported .obj file, reducing material count. When set to false, each part receives its own independent material definition. Defaults to false.
m.s: Sets whether materials should be generated per part, or per unique appearance in Roblox's exporter.

m.d: Determines how the framerate manager (FRM) manages rendering quality using a FramerateManagerMode value. When set to FramerateManagerMode.Automatic, the engine decides whether to enable FRM quality adjustment based on context (typically enabled during gameplay). When set to FramerateManagerMode.On, the FRM is always active. When set to FramerateManagerMode.Off, the FRM does not adjust quality and block culling is forced to the lowest-quality distance setting. Defaults to FramerateManagerMode.Automatic.
m.s: Specifies the behavior of the framerate manager.

m.d:
Determines which graphics rendering API Roblox uses on startup, specified as a GraphicsMode value. When set to GraphicsMode.Automatic, the engine selects the best available backend for the current platform. Available options are platform-dependent; for example, GraphicsMode.Metal is only available on macOS and GraphicsMode.Direct3D11 is only available on Windows. If an unsupported mode is selected, the engine silently falls back to GraphicsMode.Automatic. Defaults to GraphicsMode.Automatic.

Because the graphics API is initialized at startup, changing this property only takes effect after restarting Roblox Studio.
m.s: The graphics API that Roblox will use on startup.

m.d: The size in bytes of the mesh cache. Defaults to 32 MiB.
m.s: The size in bytes of the mesh cache.

m.d:
Determines the mode for the selection of detail levels for mesh parts. For a good balance between performance and fidelity, this should be set to MeshPartDetailLevel.DistanceBased (default), which is what the client uses.

Note that the MeshPart.RenderFidelity needs to be set to RenderFidelity.Automatic for this to work. If you set it to RenderFidelity.Precise, you will always see the higher resolution version and the MeshPartDetailLevel value will be ignored for that MeshPart.
m.s: Studio only. Used to visually verify the quality of `Class.MeshPart|MeshParts` at lower level of detail at close range.

m.d: If EnableFRM is set to true, this property controls the quality level in Roblox Studio.
m.s: Controls the quality level in Roblox Studio.

m.d: When set to true, Roblox Studio will automatically reload changes that are made to files in Roblox's content folder.
m.s: Whether Roblox Studio will automatically reload changes that are made to files in Roblox's `content` folder.

m.d: When set to true, a wireframe of polygons will be shown on all PartOperation objects.
m.s: Whether a wireframe of polygons will be shown on all `Class.PartOperation` objects.

m.d: If set to true, renders bounding boxes around each individual rendered entity in the scene.
m.s: Whether bounding boxes are rendered around each individual rendered entity in the scene.

m.d: Studio only. Determines which debug rendering visualization is drawn over the viewport, using a value of ViewMode. Defaults to ViewMode.None, which disables the overlay. Other values enable overdraw visualizations for geometry complexity, transparency, or decals.
m.s: Studio only. Selects a debug rendering visualization overlay for the viewport.

m.d: Returns the total number of quality levels available in the rendering quality system. Quality levels are numbered from QualityLevel.Automatic (0) through QualityLevel.Level21 (21), so this method returns 22. Use GetMaxQualityLevel() - 1 to obtain the highest numeric quality level.
m.s: Returns the maximum quality level.

r.s: The total number of quality levels available in the rendering system.

class/ReplicatedFirst.d:
ReplicatedFirst is a container whose contents are replicated to all clients (but not back to the server) before anything else. It's most commonly used to store LocalScripts and other elements that are essential for the experience's start such as loading screens.

For objects that do not need to be replicated before anything else, use the ReplicatedStorage container instead.

There are some key considerations for running LocalScripts in ReplicatedFirst:

  • Since its contents replicate before anything else in the experience, LocalScripts running in ReplicatedFirst will need to wait for any objects they require to replicate using Instance:WaitForChild()
  • Any objects that are to be used by a LocalScript in ReplicatedFirst should also be parented to ReplicatedFirst. Otherwise, they may replicate to the client late, yielding the script and negating the benefit of initial replication.
class/ReplicatedFirst.s: A container whose contents are replicated to all clients (but not back to the server) first before anything else.

m.d:
Immediately removes the default Roblox loading screen. Note that if any object has been placed in ReplicatedFirst, the default loading screen will be removed after a few seconds regardless if this method has been called or not.

You should not remove the default loading screen unless you want to display your own. If you remove the default screen without a replacement, players will be able to see geometry loading in the background.
m.s: Immediately removes the default Roblox loading screen.

class/ReplicatedStorage.d:
ReplicatedStorage is a general container service for objects that are available to both the server and connected clients. It is ideal for ModuleScript, RemoteFunction, RemoteEvent, and other objects that are useful to both server-side Scripts and client-side LocalScripts.

Objects parented to this service are fully replicated to clients, and normal replication rules apply. Any changes that are made on the client persist but aren't replicated to the server. Client changes may be overwritten if the server does something that overwrites those changes.

Certain changes on the client, such as moving an object from the Workspace to ReplicatedStorage, can lead to desynchronization issues (for example, physics updates not being replicated to the object).

LocalScripts do not run when parented to this service, even if they are Enabled; LocalScripts have various other locations where they eventually run on a Player client such as StarterPlayerScripts, StarterCharacterScripts, or StarterGui.

Similarly, Scripts do not run when parented to this service unless you change their RunContext property from the default value of Legacy. Server Scripts that run on their own should be parented to ServerScriptService instead.

If a ModuleScript within this service is required by any other script, it runs as normal. Such modules typically house code that is shared by the server and client.
class/ReplicatedStorage.s: A container service for objects that are replicated to all clients.

kid.simple: ReplicatedStorage is a storage box that BOTH the server and every player's device can see. Put things here that both sides need: ModuleScripts with shared code, RemoteEvents for sending messages, and items or effects you will clone later. Things here are not in the 3D world, so they are not drawn and do not do physics.
kid.analogy: ReplicatedStorage is like a shared bookshelf in a classroom. The teacher (server) and every student (client) can grab books from it. ServerStorage, by contrast, is the teacher's locked cabinet.
whenToUse: ModuleScripts that both Scripts and LocalScripts need to require.
RemoteEvents and RemoteFunctions, so the server and clients can talk.
Templates like tools, pets, or effects that both sides might clone.
kid.where: A service that exists on the server and all clients. Get it with `game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")`. Anything the server puts here is copied to every player.

terms.server: Roblox's computer that runs the one shared copy of the game for everyone in the server. What happens here is the truth everyone sees.
terms.client: One player's own device (computer, phone, tablet, or console). Each player has their own client.
terms.service: A special built-in object at the top of the game, like Workspace or Players. Get one with `game:GetService("Name")`.
terms.replicate: To copy from the server to every player's device. Everything in ReplicatedStorage replicates.
terms.RemoteEvent: A messenger object that lets server Scripts and LocalScripts send each other messages.
terms.template: An original object you keep tucked away and `Clone` whenever you need a new copy.

examples.title: Server clones a sword from ReplicatedStorage
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService (with a Tool named Sword in ReplicatedStorage)
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")

local swordTemplate = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("Sword")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
	player.CharacterAdded:Connect(function()
		local sword = swordTemplate:Clone()
		sword.Parent = player:WaitForChild("Backpack")
	end)
end)
explain: The Sword sits in ReplicatedStorage as a template.
Every time a player's character spawns, the server clones it.
Putting the copy in the player's Backpack gives them the tool.

gotchas: Scripts and LocalScripts do not run here (with default settings). Only ModuleScripts here run, and only when required.
Players can see everything in here, even exploiters, so never put secrets or server-only code here. Use ServerStorage or ServerScriptService for that.
Changes a client makes in ReplicatedStorage stay on that client only and are not sent to the server.

class/ReverbSoundEffect.d:
The ReverbSoundEffect simulates the effect of sounds bouncing off of several surfaces (such as walls in a room), which causes several overlapping echoes that arrive at the listener at slightly offset times.

Like all other SoundEffects, a ReverbSoundEffect can be applied either to a Sound or SoundGroup by being parented to either.
class/ReverbSoundEffect.s: Reverberates audio, simulating the effect of bouncing off walls in a room.

m.d: Range: 0.1 to 20 (default 1.5) Sets how long it takes for the reverberating echoes to fade out completely. Larger decay times simulate larger (empty) spaces
m.s: Sets how long it takes for the reverberating echoes to fade out completely.

m.d: Range: 0 to 1 (default 1) Controls how many reflections are generated.
m.s: Controls how many reflections are generated.

m.d: Range: 0 to 1 (default 1) Controls how smooth and reflective the simulated surfaces are. The lower this value, the more discrete the echoes are. At higher levels the echos will blend more.
m.s: Controls how smooth and reflective the simulated surfaces are.

m.d: Range: -80 to 10 (default -6) The output volume of the original sound.
m.s: The output volume of the original sound.

m.d: Range: -80 to 10 (default 0) The output volume of the echoed effect.
m.s: The output volume of the echoed effect.

class/RigidConstraint.d:
RigidConstraint connects two Attachments or Bones and ensures they stay in the same relative position/orientation to each other. This flexibility gives it additional functionality beyond WeldConstraint, such as attaching accessories to Attachments on a character rig.

The fastest way to create this constraint is by selecting Rigid Constraint through Studio's Create menu in the toolbar's Model tab.

Note that this tool behaves differently depending on whether you click on existing BaseParts, Attachments, or Bones after the tool is activated:

  • Clicking on an existing BasePart creates a new Attachment upon it as the intended RigidConstraint.Attachment0 or RigidConstraint.Attachment1.
  • Clicking on an existing Attachment or Bone uses that instance as the intended RigidConstraint.Attachment0 or RigidConstraint.Attachment1.

Following the second valid click, a new RigidConstraint is created to connect the two new attachments. If either the first or second click is not made on a BasePart, Attachment, or Bone, the workflow is canceled and no constraint is created.
class/RigidConstraint.s: Creates a rigid connection between two `Class.Attachment|Attachments` or `Class.Bone|Bones`.

class/RocketPropulsion.d:
The RocketPropulsion object applies force on an assembly so that it both follows and faces a target. It acts like a hybrid of BodyPosition and BodyGyro. Unlike other BodyMovers, RocketPropulsion must be instructed to begin applying or stopping force via Fire() or Abort() respectively.

You can detect when the assembly reaches its target using the ReachedTarget event which fires once the assembly is within the TargetRadius of the Target part.
class/RocketPropulsion.s: Applies a force so that an assembly follows and faces a target part.
class/RocketPropulsion.dep: This object is deprecated and should not be used for new work. Use LineForce instead, and see the legacy conversion notes.

m.d: This property determines the tendency of the assembly to face the Target. By default, this property is set to 0.7. If set to 0, the assembly will make no effort to face the target.
m.s: Determines the tendency of the assembly to face the `Class.RocketPropulsion.Target|Target`.

m.d: This property determines the upper limit of the velocity at which the assembly will move toward the Target.
m.s: Determines the maximum speed at which the assembly will move toward the `Class.RocketPropulsion.Target|Target`.

m.d: This property determines the upper limit of the thrust that may be exerted to move the assembly. Assemblies that have high mass will require more thrust in order to remain airborne and thus track the Target.
m.s: Determines the maximum amount of thrust that will be exerted to move the assembly.

m.d: This property determines the upper limit on the amount of torque that may be exerted in order to rotate the assembly towards the Target. It functions similarly to BodyGyro.MaxTorque.
m.s: Determines the maximum amount of torque that may be exerted to rotate the assembly towards the `Class.RocketPropulsion.Target|Target`.

m.d: This property determines the object towards which the RocketPropulsion will exert force/torque. If set to nil, the TargetOffset will be used instead.
m.s: Determines the object towards which the assembly should follow/face.

m.d: This property determines the world offset from the Target. It is especially useful when Target is set to nil, since this property then acts as the target position.
m.s: Determines the world offset from the `Class.RocketPropulsion.Target|Target` toward which the force/torque is exerted.

m.d: This property determines the maximum distance from the Target at which the assembly must be in order for ReachedTarget to be fired. It does not affect the exerted forces in any way.
m.s: Determines the maximum distance from the `Class.RocketPropulsion.Target|Target` at which the assembly must be in order for `Class.RocketPropulsion.ReachedTarget|ReachedTarget` to be fired.

m.d: This property is used to dampen the velocity of the assembly in order to prevent it from overshooting the Target and causing a "rubber‑banding" effect. It behaves similarly to BodyPosition.D.
m.s: Determines the dampening applied to the assembly in order to prevent it from overshooting the `Class.RocketPropulsion.Target|Target`.

m.d: This property determines how much power is used while applying force in order to reach the Target position. The higher this value, the more power will be used and the faster it will be used. This property works similarly to BodyPosition.P.
m.s: Determines how aggressive of a force is applied in reaching the `Class.RocketPropulsion.Target|Target`.

m.d: This property specifies how much dampening will be applied to the torque used to face the Target. When the assembly approaches the goal orientation, it needs to decelerate, otherwise it will rotate past the goal and have to stop and re-accelerate back toward the goal. This often creates an undesirable "rubber‑banding" effect, avoided by applying dampening. The higher this value is set, the greater the dampening curve becomes, or the slower the part will approach the goal orientation.
m.s: Determines the amount of dampening that to use in reaching the `Class.RocketPropulsion.Target|Target`.

m.d: This property determines how much power is used while applying torque in order to face the Target. The higher this value, the more power will be used and the faster it will be used.
m.s: Determines how aggressive of a torque is applied in facing the `Class.RocketPropulsion.Target|Target`.

m.d: Causes the assembly to stop moving toward its Target.
m.s: Causes the assembly to stop moving toward its `Class.RocketPropulsion.Target|Target`.

m.d: Causes the assembly to start moving toward its Target.
m.s: Causes the assembly to start moving toward its `Class.RocketPropulsion.Target|Target`.

m.dep: This function is a deprecated variant of RocketPropulsion:Fire() which should be used instead.

m.d: Fires when the assembly comes within TargetRadius of the Target.
m.s: Fires when the assembly comes within `Class.RocketPropulsion.TargetRadius|TargetRadius` of the `Class.RocketPropulsion.Target|Target`.

class/RodConstraint.d:
A RodConstraint keeps two attachments separated by its defined Length. By default, both attachments can rotate freely, although you can enable limits to restrict rotational tilt.

Note that if this constraint attaches one part (A) to another part (B) that is anchored or connected to an anchored part (Z), part A will not be locally simulated when interacting with a player.

Limits

You can limit rotation of the attachments within a cone, independently of each other, by enabling the LimitsEnabled property and setting LimitAngle0 and LimitAngle1 respectively.
class/RodConstraint.s: Keeps two attachments separated by its defined `Class.RodConstraint.Length|Length`.

m.d: The current distance between the constraint's Attachments.
m.s: The current distance between the constraint's `Class.Attachment|Attachments`.

kid.simple: Read-only: how far apart the two attachments are right now, in studs (usually very close to Length).
kid.example: print(workspace.Ceiling.RodConstraint.CurrentDistance)

m.d: The distance apart at which the constraint attempts to keep its Attachments. Measured in studs.
m.s: The distance apart at which the constraint attempts to keep its `Class.Attachment|Attachments`.

kid.simple: The distance, in studs, the rod keeps between the two attachments.
kid.example: workspace.Train.Link.RodConstraint.Length = 3

m.d: This property determines the maximum angle between the rod and Attachment0 when LimitsEnabled is true.
m.s: The maximum angle between the rod and `Class.Constraint.Attachment0|Attachment0` when `Class.RodConstraint.LimitsEnabled|LimitsEnabled` is true.

kid.simple: When LimitsEnabled is true, the biggest angle allowed between the rod and Attachment0, so that end can only tilt so far.
kid.example: workspace.Ceiling.RodConstraint.LimitAngle0 = 30

m.d: This property determines the maximum angle between the rod and Attachment1 when LimitsEnabled is true.
m.s: The maximum angle between the rod and `Class.Constraint.Attachment1|Attachment1` when `Class.RodConstraint.LimitsEnabled|LimitsEnabled` is true.

kid.simple: When LimitsEnabled is true, the biggest angle allowed between the rod and Attachment1.
kid.example: workspace.Ceiling.RodConstraint.LimitAngle1 = 30

m.d: This property determines whether the LimitAngle0 and LimitAngle1 properties control the angles between the rod and the respective attachments.
m.s: Determines whether `Class.RodConstraint.LimitAngle0|LimitAngle0` and `Class.RodConstraint.LimitAngle1|LimitAngle1` control the angles between the rod and the respective attachments.

kid.simple: If true, LimitAngle0 and LimitAngle1 restrict how far each end can tilt away from the rod.
kid.example:
local rod = workspace.Ceiling.RodConstraint
rod.LimitsEnabled = true
rod.LimitAngle0 = 45

m.d: The visualized thickness of the RodConstraint.
m.s: The visualized thickness of the `Class.RodConstraint`.

kid.simple: How thick the rod looks when drawn. Only changes the look.
kid.example: workspace.Ceiling.RodConstraint.Thickness = 0.3

kid.simple: RodConstraint keeps two attachments exactly Length studs apart, like a stiff stick between them. Unlike a rope, they cannot get closer either. Both ends can still swivel freely unless you turn on limits.
kid.analogy: RodConstraint is like a broom handle held between two hands: your hands can tilt and turn, but they always stay the same distance apart.
whenToUse: Train cars linked together
Pendulums that should not go slack
Pistons and linkages in machines
Trailers hitched to vehicles
kid.where: Make it with Instance.new("RodConstraint"), set Attachment0 and Attachment1 (one in each part) and put it in workspace. Set Visible = true to draw it.

terms.constraint: An invisible rule or connector that the physics engine follows, like 'these two parts must stay stuck together' or 'push this part upward'.
terms.attachment: A tiny invisible point you put inside a part. It has a position AND a direction (its own X, Y and Z arrows). Constraints grab parts by their attachments.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachments a constraint connects. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed or moved; Attachment1 is the other end or the goal.
terms.stud: Roblox's unit of length. A default baseplate grid square is 1 stud; a classic character is about 5 studs tall.
terms.anchored: An anchored part is frozen in place. Physics and constraint forces cannot move it. Set `part.Anchored = false` if you want a constraint to move it.
terms.unanchored: A part that physics is allowed to move. Constraints that push or pull only work on unanchored parts.
terms.limits: Stops that keep a joint from moving too far, like a door that can only swing 90 degrees.
terms.cone limit: A limit that lets an end tilt only up to a certain angle away from the rod, like moving your arm inside an ice-cream-cone shape.

examples.title: A pendulum that never goes slack
examples.code:
local ceiling = workspace:WaitForChild("Ceiling") -- anchored part
local ball = workspace:WaitForChild("Ball")       -- unanchored part

local a0 = Instance.new("Attachment")
a0.Parent = ceiling
local a1 = Instance.new("Attachment")
a1.Parent = ball

local rod = Instance.new("RodConstraint")
rod.Attachment0 = a0
rod.Attachment1 = a1
rod.Length = 8        -- always exactly 8 studs apart
rod.Visible = true
rod.Thickness = 0.2
rod.Parent = ceiling
explain: The ball always stays exactly 8 studs from the ceiling attachment.
Unlike a rope, if you push the ball up toward the ceiling, the rod pushes back; it never goes slack.

gotchas: If you want the ends to be able to get closer, use RopeConstraint instead.
Length is set in studs. If the parts start farther apart or closer than Length, they will be yanked to the right distance.

If a part is joined this way to an anchored part (or something connected to an anchored part), its physics is not calculated on the player's own device when they touch it, so it may feel slightly delayed.

class/RopeConstraint.d:
A RopeConstraint prevents two attachments from separating further than a defined Length. The attachments can move closer together than this length and both can freely rotate. This constraint can also be powered to behave as a motorized winch.

When configuring this constraint, it may be helpful to study Roblox Units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.

Winch

If a rope's WinchEnabled property is enabled, it attempts to translate the attachments to a set separation specified by WinchTarget, effectively the target length of the rope in studs. This translation is controlled by WinchSpeed, WinchResponsiveness, and WinchForce.

Note that WinchSpeed must be a positive value, used to either contract or extend the rope length to WinchTarget. Setting a negative speed will revert to 0, not reverse the winch servo direction.
class/RopeConstraint.s: Simulates rope dynamics, preventing two attachments from separating further than a defined length.

m.d: The current distance between the constraint's Attachments.

kid.where: Make it with Instance.new("RopeConstraint"), set Attachment0 and Attachment1 (one in each part) and put it in workspace. Set Visible = true to draw the rope in the game.

terms.constraint: An invisible rule or connector that the physics engine follows, like 'these two parts must stay stuck together' or 'push this part upward'.
terms.attachment: A tiny invisible point you put inside a part. It has a position AND a direction (its own X, Y and Z arrows). Constraints grab parts by their attachments.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachments a constraint connects. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed or moved; Attachment1 is the other end or the goal.
terms.stud: Roblox's unit of length. A default baseplate grid square is 1 stud; a classic character is about 5 studs tall.
terms.force: A push or pull. In Roblox it is measured in Roblox force units (mass x studs per second per second). A bigger number is a harder push.
terms.anchored: An anchored part is frozen in place. Physics and constraint forces cannot move it. Set `part.Anchored = false` if you want a constraint to move it.
terms.unanchored: A part that physics is allowed to move. Constraints that push or pull only work on unanchored parts.
terms.restitution: Bounciness, from 0 (no bounce, just stops) to 1 (bounces back as hard as it hit).
terms.winch: A motor that winds a rope in or lets it out, like on a crane or a tow truck.
terms.WinchTarget: The rope length (in studs) the winch tries to reach.
terms.responsiveness: How sharply the winch reaches its target. Higher numbers react faster.

examples.title: A swinging ball on a rope
examples.code:
local ceiling = workspace:WaitForChild("Ceiling") -- anchored part
local ball = workspace:WaitForChild("Ball")       -- unanchored part

local a0 = Instance.new("Attachment")
a0.Parent = ceiling
local a1 = Instance.new("Attachment")
a1.Parent = ball

local rope = Instance.new("RopeConstraint")
rope.Attachment0 = a0
rope.Attachment1 = a1
rope.Length = 10      -- never more than 10 studs apart
rope.Visible = true   -- draw the rope
rope.Thickness = 0.2
rope.Parent = ceiling
explain: The ball can swing anywhere within 10 studs of the ceiling attachment, like a pendulum.
If the ball is pushed toward the ceiling, the rope goes slack, just like a real rope.
Visible = true draws the rope so players can see it.

examples.title: A crane winch that lifts a crate
examples.code:
local rope = workspace:WaitForChild("Crane"):WaitForChild("RopeConstraint")

rope.WinchEnabled = true
rope.WinchForce = 100000      -- strong enough to lift the crate
rope.WinchSpeed = 4           -- reel at 4 studs per second
rope.WinchResponsiveness = 45

rope.WinchTarget = 2          -- reel in to 2 studs (lift!)
task.wait(6)
rope.WinchTarget = 15         -- let it back out to 15 studs (lower)
explain: With WinchEnabled on, the rope changes its own length toward WinchTarget.
WinchSpeed is how fast it reels, always a positive number. Whether it reels in or out depends on whether the target is shorter or longer.
WinchForce must be more than the crate's weight (mass x 196.2) to lift it.

gotchas: A rope only stops things from getting FARTHER apart. To keep things a fixed distance (no slack), use RodConstraint.
Ropes are invisible in the game unless Visible = true.
WinchSpeed must be positive. A negative speed becomes 0; it does not reverse the winch. Change WinchTarget instead.
If the winch cannot lift something, raise WinchForce.

class/Rotate.d: The Rotate object is used to allow rotation between two parts. Most commonly created through the SurfaceType.Hinge on a BasePart. If created like this, the rotation will be about the normal vector from the face of the part the hinge is placed on. If created through a script, the axis and point of rotation can be defined arbitrarily.
class/Rotate.dep: This class works alongside the deprecated SurfaceType and should not be used for future work; use HingeConstraint instead.

class/RotateP.d:
A RotateP object joins two parts together and allows rotation about a set axis. The joint will attempt to rotate the two parts until a desired rotational position is reached. This object is most commonly created by the SurfaceType.SteppingMotor on a BasePart. If created through a script, behavior is still governed by the surface input of JointInstance.Part0.

The three inputs of note are as follows:

  • NoInput — The joint will not rotate under its own power. It can still be rotated by external forces (such as from a character pushing one of the parts).

  • Constant — The joint will rotate based on the ParamB property of JointInstance.Part0. This rotation is measured in radians per physics frame (which is approximately 1/60th of a second).

  • Sin — The joint will rotate based on the ParamA and ParamB properties of JointInstance.Part0.
class/RotateP.dep: This class works alongside the deprecated SurfaceType and should not be used for future work; use HingeConstraint instead.

class/RotateV.d:
A RotateV object joins two parts together and allows rotation about a set axis. This object is most commonly created by the SurfaceType.Motor on a BasePart. If created through a script, behavior is still governed by the surface input of JointInstance.Part0.

The three inputs of note are as follows:

  • NoInput — The joint will not rotate under its own power. It can still be rotated by external forces (such as from a character pushing one of the parts).

  • Constant — The joint will rotate based on the ParamB property of JointInstance.Part0. This rotation is measured in radians per physics frame (which is approximately 1/60th of a second).

  • Sin — The joint will rotate based on the ParamA and ParamB properties of JointInstance.Part0.
class/RotateV.s: Joins two parts and allows rotation driven by angular velocity from the Motor surface type.

class/RunService.d:
RunService contains methods and events for time management as well as for managing the context in which an experience or script is running. Methods like IsClient(), IsServer(), and IsStudio() can help you determine under what context code is running. These methods are useful for ModuleScripts that may be required by both client and server scripts. Furthermore, IsStudio() can be used to add special behaviors for in‑Studio testing.

RunService also houses events that allow your code to adhere to the engine's frame‑by‑frame loop, such as PreRender, PreAnimation, PreSimulation, PostSimulation, and Heartbeat. Selecting the proper event to use for any case is important, so you should read Task Scheduler to make an informed decision.

class/RunService.s: Service responsible for all runtime activity and progression of time.

m.d:
An RunState value that reflects whether the game's simulation is stopped, running, or paused. Reading reports the current state; setting it transitions the simulation, equivalent to RunService:Run(), RunService:Pause(), and RunService:Stop() for the corresponding states. Defaults to RunState.Stopped. Setting this property requires Plugin security.

The state reported here backs the context methods on RunService: it is Running when IsRunning() returns true, and Stopped when IsEdit() returns true.
m.s: The current run state of the game's simulation.

kid.simple: Tells you if the game's simulation is Stopped, Running or Paused. Only plugins can change it; normal scripts can only read it.
kid.example:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
print(RunService.RunState) -- Enum.RunState.Running while you play

m.d:
BindToAnimation() binds a custom function to be called at a fixed frequency which is independent of the frame rate. When Workspace.UseFixedSimulation is enabled, these functions are invoked before Animators update, making this the fixed-frequency counterpart to PreAnimation. When fixed simulation is disabled, they instead run immediately before BindToSimulation() callbacks, so no pre-animation ordering should be assumed. In the server authority model, bound functions will also get called when the client needs to resimulate.

Like BindToSimulation(), the bound function is meant for physics controllers and prediction, so an error will trigger if you read or write from unsynchronized properties or call an unsynchronized method. This error is meant to help guide you in writing a pure, synchronized simulation.

To synchronize inaccessible properties, you should store the relevant data in attributes and update the relevant property in PostSimulation or RenderStepped by reading from attributes. This will leverage attribute synchronization to keep the property fully synchronized through the rollback mechanism.
m.s: Binds a custom function to be called at a fixed frequency before Animators update when fixed simulation is enabled, or immediately before `BindToSimulation` callbacks otherwise.

p.s: The function to call. This function will be passed one parameter called deltaTime, which shows the elapsed time since the callback's previous invocation.
Optional StepFrequency value indicating the frequency at which to call the bound function. Defaults to StepFrequency.Hz30.

Optional priority of the binding as an integer; it determines the order in which bound functions are called within a simulation step. Lower numbers are called first. If two bindings have the same priority, the order between them is unspecified. Defaults to 2000.

r.s: A RBXScriptConnection that can be disconnected to unregister the callback.

kid.simple: An advanced tool for physics prediction games. It calls your function a fixed number of times per second (default 30), no matter the frame rate, right before animations update. It returns a connection you can disconnect. Most games do not need this.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript (advanced; most games do not need this)
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
local connection = RunService:BindToAnimation(function(deltaTime)
    -- adjust animation-related values here, 30 times per second
end, Enum.StepFrequency.Hz30)
-- later: connection:Disconnect()
kid.gotcha: Inside the bound function you may only touch properties that are kept in sync for prediction; touching others causes an error.

m.d:
The BindToRenderStep() function binds a custom function to be called at a specific time during the render step. There are three main arguments: name, priority, and what function to call.

As it is linked to the client's rendering process, BindToRenderStep() can only be called on the client.

Name

The name parameter is a label for the binding and can be used with RunService:UnbindFromRenderStep() if the binding is no longer needed.

local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

local function functionToBind() end

-- Bind the function above to the binding named "tempBinding"
RunService:BindToRenderStep("tempBinding", 1, functionToBind)
-- Unbind the function bound to "tempBinding"
RunService:UnbindFromRenderStep("tempBinding")
Priority

The priority of the binding is an integer; it determines when during the render step to call the custom function. The lower this number, the sooner the custom function will be called. If two bindings have the same priority, the engine will randomly pick one to run first. The default control scripts run with these specific priorities:

  • Player Input: 100
  • Camera Controls: 200 For convenience; the RenderPriority enum can be used to determine the integer value to set a binding. For example, to make a binding right before the default camera update, simply subtract 1 from the camera priority level.

When using RenderPriority, remember to use .Value at the end of the desired enum. RunService:BindToRenderStep() will not work if just the enum is used on its own.

local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

local function beforeCamera(delta)
    -- Code in here will run before the default camera script
end

RunService:BindToRenderStep("Before camera", Enum.RenderPriority.Camera.Value - 1, beforeCamera)
Custom Function and Delta Time

The last argument (function) is the custom function to call. This function will be passed one parameter called deltaTime which shows how much time passed between the beginning of the previous render step and the beginning of the current render step.

All rendering updates will wait until the code in the render step finishes. Make sure that any code called by BindToRenderStep() runs quickly and efficiently; if code takes too long, the experience visuals will be choppy.
m.s: Given a string name of a function and a priority, this method binds the function to `Class.RunService.PreRender`.

p.s: Label for the binding which can be used with Unbind if the binding is no longer needed.

Priority of the binding as an integer; it determines when during the render step to call the custom function. The lower this number, the sooner the custom function will be called. If two bindings have the same priority, the engine will randomly pick one to run first.
The custom function being bound.

kid.simple: Attaches your function to the moment just before each frame is drawn, with a name and a priority number that controls the order. Lower numbers run first. Player input runs at 100 and the camera at 200, so you can run code right before or after the camera moves. Client only.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

local function beforeCamera(deltaTime)
    -- runs every frame, just before the default camera updates
end

-- .Value turns the enum into its number (Camera = 200, so this is 199)
RunService:BindToRenderStep("MyBeforeCamera", Enum.RenderPriority.Camera.Value - 1, beforeCamera)

-- to stop it later:
-- RunService:UnbindFromRenderStep("MyBeforeCamera")
kid.gotcha: Pass a number, not the enum itself: use `Enum.RenderPriority.Camera.Value`. Keep the code fast, because the frame cannot be drawn until it finishes.

m.d:
BindToSimulation() binds a custom function to be called at a fixed frequency which is independent of the frame rate. In the server authority model, bound functions will also get called when the client needs to resimulate. This method is only available when Workspace.UseFixedSimulation is enabled.

Note that since the bound function is meant for physics controllers and prediction, an error will trigger if you read or write from unsynchronized properties or call an unsynchronized method. This error is meant to help guide you in writing a pure, synchronized simulation.

To synchronize inaccessible properties, you should store the relevant data in attributes and update the relevant property in PostSimulation or RenderStepped by reading from attributes. This will leverage attribute synchronization to keep the property fully synchronized through the rollback mechanism.
m.s: Binds a custom function to be called at a fixed frequency which is independent of the frame rate.

p.s: The function to call. This function will be passed one parameter called deltaTime which shows how much time passed between the beginning of the previous simulation step and the beginning of the current simulation step.
Optional StepFrequency value indicating the frequency at which to call the bound function. If not provided, the default frequency will be used.

Optional priority of the binding as an integer; it determines the order in which bound functions are called within a simulation step. Lower numbers are called first. If two bindings have the same priority, the order between them is unspecified. Defaults to 2000.

r.s: An RBXScriptConnection that can be disconnected to unbind the function from the simulation step.

kid.simple: An advanced tool for physics prediction. It calls your function a fixed number of times per second (default 30), separate from the frame rate. Only works when `Workspace.UseFixedSimulation` is turned on. Returns a connection to disconnect it.
kid.example:
-- Advanced: requires Workspace.UseFixedSimulation to be enabled
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
local connection = RunService:BindToSimulation(function(deltaTime)
    -- push a vehicle, for example, 60 times per second
end, Enum.StepFrequency.Hz60)
kid.gotcha: Reading or writing properties that are not kept in sync for prediction inside this function causes an error.

m.d: Clients can use this method to check the PredictionStatus of a specific context instance, useful for debugging scripts affecting multiple instances (vehicle controllers, custom physics, etc.) where some might be predicted and others might not. This method is also useful for debugging and observing the effects of PredictionMode.Automatic prediction mode.
m.s: Checks the `Enum.PredictionStatus` of a specific context instance, useful for debugging scripts affecting multiple instances where some might be predicted and others might not.

kid.simple: Advanced, client only. Tells you whether an object is currently being predicted (guessed ahead by the player's device) in a server authority game. Useful for debugging.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript (advanced)
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
print(RunService:GetPredictionStatus(workspace.Car))

m.d:
If the code that invoked this method is running in a client context (in a LocalScript, in a ModuleScript required by a LocalScript, or in a Script with RunContext set to RunContext.Client), this method will return true. In all other cases, this method will return false.

If this method returns true, the current environment can access client‑only features like RunService.PreRender or Players.LocalPlayer.
m.s: Returns whether the current environment is running on the client.

r.s: Whether the current environment is running the client.

kid.simple: Returns true if this code is running on a player's device (a LocalScript, or a ModuleScript loaded by one). Handy inside ModuleScripts that both sides use.
kid.example:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
if RunService:IsClient() then
    print("I am running on a player's device")
end

m.d:
This method returns whether the current environment is in "edit" mode, for example in Studio when the experience is not running.

IsEdit() will return the inverse of IsRunning(), except when the simulation has been paused, in which case both methods will return false.
m.s: Returns whether the current environment is in `Edit` mode.

r.s: Whether the current environment is in "edit" mode.

kid.simple: Returns true when you are in Studio building (edit mode) and the game is not running. Mostly useful for plugins.
kid.example:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
print(RunService:IsEdit()) -- false while playtesting

m.d: Returns true if the engine is currently replaying simulation steps after detecting a misprediction in the server authority model; returns false otherwise. When the server's authoritative state diverges from the client's predicted state, the client rolls back and rapidly resimulates all affected steps within a single frame. During that resimulation pass, BindToSimulation() callbacks and property-changed signals fire again for each replayed step, which can cause unwanted side effects such as duplicate sound playback or redundant network requests.
m.s: Returns whether the client is currently in a resimulation step after a misprediction in the server authority model.

r.s: Whether the engine is currently resimulating.

kid.simple: Advanced. Returns true while the player's device is replaying physics steps because its guess was wrong (server authority). Use it to avoid doing things twice, like playing a sound again.
kid.example:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
local sound = workspace:WaitForChild("Ding") -- a Sound in Workspace
if not RunService:IsResimulating() then
    sound:Play() -- only play once, not again during a replay
end

m.d: This method returns whether a Run playtest has been initiated in Studio. It will continue to return true if the simulation has been paused using the Pause button; however, once it has been stopped using the Stop button, it will revert to returning false. Note that Studio only enters "run" mode when a Run playtest (without the user's player character) is initiated. Also note that this method will return false if the simulation was started using RunService:Run().
m.s: Returns whether a **Run** playtest has been initiated in Studio.

r.s: Whether a Run playtest has been initiated in Studio.

kid.simple: Returns true if Studio is in a Run test (the kind with no player character). It is false for a normal Play test.
kid.example:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
print(RunService:IsRunMode())

m.d: Returns whether the experience is currently running. IsRunning() will always return the inverse of IsEdit() except when the simulation has been paused, in which case both methods will return false.
m.s: Returns whether the experience is currently running.

r.s: Whether the experience is currently running.

kid.simple: Returns true if the game is currently running (playing), false in edit mode or while paused.
kid.example:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
print(RunService:IsRunning()) -- true in a live game

In all other cases, this method will return false.

If this function returns true, then the current environment can access server‑only features like ServerStorage or ServerScriptService.

m.s: Pauses the experience's simulation if it is running, suspending physics and scripts.

game:GetService("RunService"):Pause()

m.d: Sets the prediction mode for an Instance (context) to an PredictionMode value. Mismatches between the physics properties or attributes for predicted instances will cause a rollback and resimulation on the client. Can only be called on the client.
m.s: Sets the prediction mode for an `Class.Instance` to an `Enum.PredictionMode` value.

p.s: The Instance for which to set the prediction mode.
The PredictionMode to set for the context instance.

kid.simple: Advanced, client only. Chooses whether the player's device should predict (guess ahead) the movement of an object in a server authority game.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript (advanced)
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
RunService:SetPredictionMode(workspace.Car, Enum.PredictionMode.Automatic)

m.d:
This method stops the experience's simulation if it is running. When the simulation is stopped, IsRunning() will return false and IsEdit() will return true.

In contrast to the Stop button in Studio, calling this method will not restore the experience to the state it was in prior to the simulation being run. This means any changes made to the experience by the physics simulation and scripts will persist after the simulation has ended.
m.s: Stops the experience's simulation if it is running.

kid.simple: Stops the simulation. Only plugins can use this. Unlike Studio's Stop button, it does not undo changes made while running.
kid.example:
-- Plugin only
game:GetService("RunService"):Stop()

m.d:
Given a name of a function sent to BindToRenderStep(), this method will unbind the function from being called during PreRender. This is used to unbind bound functions once they are no longer needed, or when they no longer need to fire every step.

If there is no bound function by the given name, this method takes no action and continues without raising an error.
m.s: Unbinds a function that was bound to the render loop using `Class.RunService:BindToRenderStep()`.

p.s: The name of the function being unbound.

kid.simple: Removes a function you added with `BindToRenderStep`, using the same name. If no binding has that name, nothing happens (no error).
kid.example:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
RunService:BindToRenderStep("Spin", 300, function(dt) end)
task.wait(5)
RunService:UnbindFromRenderStep("Spin") -- stop after 5 seconds

m.d:
The Heartbeat event fires every frame, after the physics simulation has completed. The deltaTime argument indicates the time that has elapsed since the previous frame.

This event is when most scripts run. It occurs at the end of each frame and it's also when any waiting scripts are executed, such as those scheduled with the task library. Heartbeat is commonly used for periodic tasks, such as updating core game systems like health regeneration.

Following this step, the engine sends property updates and events to the server or clients which are later received as part of the replication receive step.
m.s: Fires every frame, after the physics simulation has completed.

p.s: The time (in seconds) that has elapsed since the previous frame.

kid.simple: Fires every frame, at the END of the frame, after physics has moved everything. Gives you deltaTime (seconds since the last frame). This is the most common frame event and works on both server and client. Waiting scripts (like `task.wait`) also wake up at this moment.
kid.example:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
local humanoid = nil -- set this to a player's Humanoid

RunService.Heartbeat:Connect(function(deltaTime)
    -- regenerate 2 health per second
    if humanoid and humanoid.Health < humanoid.MaxHealth then
        humanoid.Health = math.min(humanoid.Health + 2 * deltaTime, humanoid.MaxHealth)
    end
end)

m.d:
With server authority enabled, the Misprediction event fires when a received server state differs from the predicted state.

Use this event to build debugging tools that inspect misprediction data programmatically. For example, a plugin could listen for this event and track which instances are frequently mispredicting, what properties are diverging, and by how much.

Instances Array

Each entry in the instances array is a table with the following structure:

Field Type Description
Instance Instance The instance that was mispredicted.
Properties dictionary? Properties that were mispredicted. Each key is a property name mapping to a table with the client's Predicted and owner's/server's Authoritative values as captured on the step when the client first mispredicted the owner's value. Only present if there are property mismatches.
Attributes dictionary? Attributes that were mispredicted. Each key is a property name mapping to a table with the client's Predicted and owner's/server's Authoritative values as captured on the step when the client first mispredicted the owner's value. Only present if there are attribute mismatches.
Stats Dictionary

The stats dictionary contains the following fields:

Field Type Description
ResimulationTime number The time spent during resimulation (or the amount of time rolled back).
Code Sample
m.s: In the server authority model, fires during prediction when the engine detects that the client has diverged from the server's authoritative state. Intended for plugin-based debugging.

p.s: The time (in seconds) from the start of simulation at which the client's predicted state first diverged from the server's authoritative state.
An array of tables, each describing an Instance that was mispredicted. See below for the structure of each entry.
A dictionary of statistics about the misprediction. See below for the structure.

kid.simple: Advanced. In a server authority game, fires when the server says the player's device guessed wrong. It gives details (time, which objects, stats) so you can build debugging tools.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript (advanced)
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
RunService.Misprediction:Connect(function(time, instances, stats)
    print("Misprediction! Objects affected:", #instances)
end)

m.d:
The PostSimulation event fires every frame, after the physics simulation has completed. The deltaTimeSim argument indicates the time that the current frame has stepped the physics simulation, not accounting for physics throttling. This may deviate from the actual time between frames in Studio edit mode or when framerate is very low.

This event is useful for making final adjustments to the outcome of the simulation. Following this phase, the engine triggers the Heartbeat event.
m.s: Fires every frame, after the physics simulation has completed.

p.s: The time (in seconds) that the current frame has stepped the physics simulation, not accounting for physics throttling.

kid.simple: Fires every frame right AFTER physics has finished moving things. Good for final fixes to where physics put things. Gives the physics step time (deltaTimeSim). Heartbeat comes right after this.
kid.example:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
local ball = workspace:WaitForChild("Ball")

RunService.PostSimulation:Connect(function(deltaTimeSim)
    -- keep the ball from flying above height 100
    if ball.Position.Y > 100 then
        ball.AssemblyLinearVelocity = Vector3.zero
    end
end)

m.d:
The PreAnimation event fires every frame, prior to the physics simulation but after rendering. The deltaTimeSim argument indicates the time that the current frame has stepped animations.

This event is useful for modifying animation objects, such as adjusting their speed or priority. Once the PreAnimation event is complete, the engine proceeds to run these animations, updating the joint transforms which will later be used to update objects during the physics simulation.

After animations are stepped, the engine triggers the PreSimulation event.
m.s: Fires every frame, prior to the physics simulation but after rendering.

p.s: The time (in seconds) that the current frame has stepped animations.

kid.simple: Fires every frame just before animations are moved forward. Useful for changing animation things like their speed. Gives deltaTimeSim, the time this frame moves animations by.
kid.example:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
RunService.PreAnimation:Connect(function(deltaTimeSim)
    -- e.g. adjust an AnimationTrack's speed here
end)

m.d:
The PreRender event (replacement for RenderStepped) fires every frame, prior to the frame being rendered. The deltaTimeRender argument indicates the time that has elapsed since the previous frame.

This event allows you to run code and update the world before it's drawn on a player's screen. This is useful for last‑minute adjustments such as changing object positions, updating animations, or preparing visual effects, but it should be used sparingly as the engine cannot start to render the frame until code running in this event has finished executing.

As PreRender is client-side, it can only be used in a LocalScript, in a ModuleScript required by a LocalScript, or in a Script with RunContext set to RunContext.Client.
m.s: Fires every frame, prior to the frame being rendered.

p.s: The time (in seconds) that has elapsed since the previous frame.

kid.simple: Fires every frame just BEFORE the picture is drawn on the player's screen. Best for things the player looks at: camera movement, smooth visual effects, objects that follow the mouse. Client only. It replaces the older `RenderStepped`.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
local part = workspace:WaitForChild("Floaty")
local startY = part.Position.Y
local t = 0

RunService.PreRender:Connect(function(deltaTime)
    t += deltaTime
    -- bob up and down by 1 stud using a sine wave
    part.Position = Vector3.new(part.Position.X, startY + math.sin(t * 2), part.Position.Z)
end)
kid.gotcha: The screen waits for your code to finish before drawing, so slow code here makes the game choppy.

m.d:
The PreSimulation event (replacement for Stepped) fires every frame, prior to the physics simulation. The deltaTimeSim argument indicates the time that the current frame will step the physics simulation, not accounting for physics throttling. This may deviate from the actual time between frames in Studio edit mode or when framerate is very low.

This event is useful for adjusting properties like velocity or forces just before they're applied as part of the simulation. The simulation then runs, potentially multiple times, as the physics solver runs at a higher frequency than other engine systems. Once this is complete, the PostSimulation event is fired.
m.s: Fires every frame, prior to the physics simulation.

p.s: The time (in seconds) that the current frame will step the physics simulation, not accounting for physics throttling.

kid.simple: Fires every frame just BEFORE physics runs. Best for changing velocity or forces so physics uses your new values right away. Gives deltaTimeSim, how much time physics will move forward this frame. It replaces the older `Stepped`.
kid.example:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
local ball = workspace:WaitForChild("Ball")

RunService.PreSimulation:Connect(function(deltaTimeSim)
    -- keep pushing the ball forward at 20 studs per second
    ball.AssemblyLinearVelocity = Vector3.new(20, ball.AssemblyLinearVelocity.Y, 0)
end)

m.d:
Fires every frame, prior to the frame being rendered.

Migration Note

This event has been superseded by PreRender which should be used for new work.
m.s: Fires every frame, prior to the frame being rendered.

p.s: The time (in seconds) that has elapsed since the previous frame.

kid.simple: The older version of `PreRender`. Fires every frame before the frame is drawn, client only, and gives deltaTime. It still works, but use `PreRender` for new code.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript (prefer PreRender in new code)
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
RunService.RenderStepped:Connect(function(deltaTime)
    print("frame took", deltaTime, "seconds")
end)

m.d:
When server authority is enabled, the Rollback event fires after the engine detects a misprediction and rolls back all eligible state (properties, attributes, and related physics and animation state), but before the engine resimulates the rolled-back steps.

Use this event to update state in your place that wouldn't otherwise be rolled back after a misprediction. For example, if you maintain gameplay state that can't be stored in a property or attribute with simulation access, you can listen for this event, compare the rolled-back-to step against your farthest-reached step, and rewind your custom state accordingly.
m.s: In the server authority model, this fires after rolling back the predicted state due to a misprediction, but before resimulation begins.

p.s: The time (in seconds) that we are rolling back to.

kid.simple: Advanced. In a server authority game, fires after the player's device rewinds because it guessed wrong, but before it replays. Use it to rewind your own saved game data too.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript (advanced)
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
RunService.Rollback:Connect(function(time)
    print("Rewound to time", time)
end)

m.d:
Fires every frame, prior to the physics simulation.

Migration Note

This event has been superseded by PreSimulation which should be used for new work.
m.s: Fires every frame, prior to the physics simulation.

p.s: The duration (in seconds) that RunService has been running for.
The time (in seconds) that has elapsed since the previous frame.

kid.simple: The older version of `PreSimulation`. Fires every frame before physics runs. It gives two numbers: the total time the game has run, and deltaTime. Still works, but use `PreSimulation` for new code.
kid.example:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
RunService.Stepped:Connect(function(totalTime, deltaTime)
    print(totalTime, deltaTime)
end)
kid.gotcha: The FIRST value is total time, not deltaTime. Many people mix these up.

kid.simple: A game does not run smoothly like a movie in real life. It draws a new picture, called a frame, about 60 times every second. RunService lets your code run once every frame, so you can make smooth motion, timers and checks. It also tells you WHERE your code is running: on the server, on a player's device, or in Studio.
kid.analogy: RunService is like the drummer in a band. Every beat (frame), it hits the drum and everyone who is listening (your connected functions) does their next little step. It also tells you how long it has been since the last beat, so you can keep in time even if the drummer speeds up or slows down.
whenToUse: Move or spin something smoothly every frame
Make a camera or object follow something (use `PreRender` in a LocalScript)
Run a check over and over very quickly, like a timer or health regeneration (use `Heartbeat`)
Change forces or velocity just before physics runs (use `PreSimulation`)
Find out if code is running on the server, the client, or in Studio (`IsServer`, `IsClient`, `IsStudio`)
kid.where: Server and client. Get it with game:GetService("RunService"). `PreRender`, `RenderStepped` and `BindToRenderStep` only work on the client (a LocalScript), because only players' devices draw pictures.

terms.frame: One picture the game draws on your screen. Roblox tries to draw about 60 frames each second. Each frame, the game also moves physics, plays animations and runs waiting scripts.
terms.frame rate (FPS): How many frames are drawn each second. 60 FPS means a new frame about every 0.0167 seconds. A slow phone might only manage 30 FPS, and some fast computers do more.
terms.delta time (deltaTime, dt): How many seconds passed since the last frame. At 60 FPS it is about 0.0167. At 30 FPS it is about 0.033. Multiply your speed by it so things move at the same speed on fast and slow devices.
terms.physics simulation: The part of the engine that makes unanchored things fall, bounce, roll and bump into each other.
terms.render: To draw the picture on the screen.
terms.client: The player's own computer, phone or console. LocalScripts run here.
terms.server: Roblox's computer that runs the game for everyone at once. Scripts in ServerScriptService run here.
terms.event: A signal that something happened. You `:Connect` a function and it runs every time the event fires.
terms.connection: What you get back from `:Connect`. Call `:Disconnect()` on it to stop your function from running.
terms.bind: To attach your function to a moment in the frame so the engine calls it for you.
terms.priority: A number that sets the order. Lower numbers run first.
terms.Studio: Roblox Studio, the program you use to build games.
terms.ModuleScript: A script that holds shared code other scripts can load with `require`.
terms.prediction / server authority: An advanced setup where the player's device guesses (predicts) what will happen and the server later says what really happened. If the guess was wrong (a misprediction), the device rewinds (rolls back) and replays (resimulates). Most games do not need this.
terms.Hz (hertz): Times per second. 30 Hz means 30 times every second.

examples.title: Move a part smoothly using deltaTime
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService (needs an anchored Part named MovingPart in Workspace)
examples.code:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

local part = workspace:WaitForChild("MovingPart")
part.Anchored = true

local SPEED = 10 -- studs per SECOND (not per frame!)

RunService.Heartbeat:Connect(function(deltaTime)
    -- distance this frame = speed x time since last frame
    -- at 60 FPS: 10 x 0.0167 = about 0.167 studs this frame
    -- at 30 FPS: 10 x 0.033  = about 0.33 studs this frame
    -- either way, after 1 second the part has moved 10 studs
    part.Position = part.Position + Vector3.new(SPEED * deltaTime, 0, 0)
end)
explain: `Heartbeat` fires once every frame and gives us `deltaTime`, the seconds since the last frame.
We want the part to move 10 studs every second, so each frame we move it `SPEED * deltaTime` studs along the X direction.
A fast computer has more frames but smaller steps; a slow one has fewer frames but bigger steps. Both end up moving 10 studs per second, so the game is fair for everybody.
If you just added 0.5 every frame instead, a 120 FPS computer would move the part 4 times faster than a 30 FPS phone. That is why we use deltaTime.

examples.title: Spin a coin smoothly on the player's screen
examples.place: LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts (needs an anchored Part named Coin in Workspace)
examples.code:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

local coin = workspace:WaitForChild("Coin")
local TURN_SPEED = math.rad(180) -- half a turn per second, turned into radians

RunService.PreRender:Connect(function(deltaTime)
    -- rotate a little around the coin's up axis each frame
    coin.CFrame = coin.CFrame * CFrame.Angles(0, TURN_SPEED * deltaTime, 0)
end)
explain: `PreRender` runs right before each frame is drawn, so changes look perfectly smooth on screen. It only works on the client, so this is a LocalScript.
`math.rad(180)` turns 180 degrees into radians, the angle unit Roblox uses (a full circle is about 6.28 radians).
Each frame we turn the coin by speed times deltaTime, so it turns exactly half a circle every second on any device.
Because a LocalScript changed it, only this player sees the coin spin. That is fine for decoration.

examples.title: A simple countdown timer that you can stop
examples.code:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

local timeLeft = 10 -- seconds
local connection

connection = RunService.Heartbeat:Connect(function(deltaTime)
    timeLeft -= deltaTime -- take away the time that passed
    if timeLeft <= 0 then
        print("Time is up!")
        connection:Disconnect() -- stop running every frame
    end
end)
explain: We store the connection so we can stop it later.
Each frame we subtract deltaTime, so after 10 real seconds `timeLeft` reaches 0 no matter the frame rate.
`connection:Disconnect()` stops the function from being called again. Always disconnect frame loops you no longer need.

gotchas: Forgetting deltaTime: moving by a fixed amount each frame makes speed depend on the player's FPS. Always multiply by deltaTime.
Heavy code inside frame events runs 60 times a second and can make the game laggy. Keep it short.
`PreRender`, `RenderStepped` and `BindToRenderStep` only work in client code (LocalScripts). Using them on the server will not work.
Use `PreRender` and `PreSimulation` in new code. `RenderStepped` and `Stepped` are older names that still work but have been replaced.
Changing a part in a LocalScript only changes it for that player. Other players will not see it.
Frame connections keep running until you `:Disconnect()` them or the script is destroyed.
In frame order: PreRender (draw prep), then PreAnimation, then PreSimulation, then physics runs, then PostSimulation, then Heartbeat.
